idiom_name: def step(...): this.type = { ...; this } - singleton return type preserved for subclasses; stdlib mutable.Builder
implementation_notes: Scala answers the fluent interface's hardest typing problem in the language itself: declaring a step's result as this.type (the singleton type of the receiver) means one definition returns the concrete receiver in every subclass, so a chain never degrades to the base type - the problem that forces covariant overrides in Java and CRTP in C++. The standard library uses the same mechanism for collections: scala.collection.mutable.Builder#addOne and += return this.type and result() is the terminal operation, with ImmutableBuilder adding reusable builders for immutable collections. What replaces the classic hand-written chain for configuration: named arguments and default parameters on case-class constructors plus copy, so most call sites never need a builder at all; keep the this.type chain for objects that genuinely accumulate steps, and an ordinary generic return type if a step produces a new value rather than the receiver.
pitfalls: this.type is the receiver's singleton type, so a step that returns a new instance cannot declare it; immutable fluent APIs must instead carry an explicit generic self type (or declare the concrete type), which is why Scala offers both shapes.

A this.type chain started from a variable whose static type is the base class only exposes the base type's steps, so the chain must begin at the concrete type (or the factory must return the concrete type).
Collapsing a configuration into one expression hides the intermediate object from the debugger and from println-based inspection of a partially applied chain.
